payload.rationale: Both sides debated at a high level with consistent citation, direct clash, and disciplined extension. PRO built a coherent spine: biological humanity of the embryo (Mayo Clinic), the act/omission distinction (killing vs. declining to aid), duty created by causing dependency (driver/sea-captain analogies), and Safe Haven off-ramps. PRO's strongest recurring move was the act/omission line, sharpened well in ping 9 with the point that standard procedures act directly on the fetal body rather than merely separating. But CON neutralized PRO's pillars more often than the reverse. CON's decisive turn came in ping 2: PRO cited the Unborn Victims of Violence Act for 'legal incoherence,' and CON quoted Section 1841(c)'s explicit consent exclusion (Cornell) to show the statute draws its line exactly at the woman's consent — turning PRO's own evidence against him, a textbook refute-with-citation that PRO never recovered. CON's central asymmetry — that the law nowhere compels even a parent to surrender blood, marrow, or a kidney to a born child (McFall v. Shimp, a real and correctly deployed case) — was pressed every turn and PRO never met CON's repeated burden challenge to produce a single precedent compelling bodily use. PRO's conscription rebuttals (jury duty, draft, quarantine, taxation) were real but CON correctly distinguished them as partial intrusions short of nine-month bodily occupation, a distinction PRO waved at but did not dismantle. On the empirical layer, CON sustained the WHO unsafe-abortion data and Poland fatalities (Izabela/Agnieszka), while PRO's Malta/Poland counter (maternal care, not legality, is the lifesaver) landed a genuine confounder hit and CON conceded the Southern-disparity point as a partial wash. Net: PRO won that a living human organism exists (CON conceded it freely), but that was never the contested premise; CON won the contested premise — whether that fact licenses state conscription of a body — and defended it more consistently with turned and uncontradicted evidence.
payload.persuasion_notes: Principle 2 (clash) was the deciding axis: CON engaged PRO's last point first in nearly every ping and turned PRO's own statute (UVVA consent clause) and analogies, whereas PRO twice relabeled rather than answered CON's no-bodily-donation-precedent challenge. Principle 3 (cite-to-refute): both sides honored it — CON's UVVA/McFall/WHO citations and PRO's Guttmacher/Commonwealth Fund citations were real and on-point, so no falsehood penalty applied to either; PRO's Malta confounder was properly cited and scored as a genuine hit. Principle 4 (dropped arguments): CON's core asymmetry — law compels no one, not even parents, to surrender internal organs — went without an effective answer across multiple turns and stands as the round's heaviest surviving weight, while PRO's act/omission distinction was contested but not dropped. Principle 1 (persuasion not truth): judged independent of the moral question; CON simply defended its contested premise with more turned evidence and fewer concessions. No tie per Principle 5; CON's higher Clash and the conceded-by-default conscription asymmetry break it for CON.
